newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Alliance condemns Irish bid for Wilson & Horton.
newsitem.headline: NZ Alliance condemns Irish bid for Wilson & Horton.

text.p: New Zealand's left-wing Alliance on Tuesday condemned a bid for publisher Wilson and Horton by Ireland's Independent Newspapers Plc as a form of "cultural imperialism".
But a senior Labour member of parliament said that party's policy to examine foreign and cross-media ownership should not be of concern to Independent.

Independent on Monday said it would make a full takeover bid for Wilson and Horton at NZ$10.50 a share via a written offer and stand in the market just days before New Zealand's October 12 general election.

Alliance broadcasting spokesperson Pam Corkery said the bid for W&H, whose New Zealand Herald is the country's highest-circulation newspaper, illustrated the total absence of controls on cross-media ownership.
"The domination of our media by private owners is a form of cultural imperialism," she said in a statement.
"The sell-off of our media is more insidious in some ways than the sale of land, because media moguls sitting in offices overseas make decisions about the information we receive here."
Independent already holds 22.6 percent of Wilson and Horton and the same amount is held by family trusts linked to Independent's major shareholder Tony O'Reilly.

Independent also has 25 percent of Australian Provincial Newspapers Holdings Ltd which, along with Wilson and Horton and Clear Channel Communications Inc of the United States, bought Radio New Zealand's commercial stations earlier this year for NZ$89 million.
The main opposition Labour Party earlier this month promised a probe into cross-media ownership and the degree of foreign control if its wins power next month.
But third-ranking Labour MP Steve Maharey said Labour's policy "does not mean Tony O'Reilly should be on the phone worried about a forced sell-down".
Maharey said: "The working party to examine these issues would look to the future, not the past."
He said it was the general view of the the Labour caucus that a diversity of ownership of the media was good, but it had never said there should be a sell-down to achieve it.
"Those things are an impossibility," he said.

Wilson and Horton's New Zealand Herald on Tuesday reported Independent deputy chairman John Meagher had tried to contact all the main political parties before the announcement of the offer, but had only managed to contact Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who he said had been "extremely polite and courteous".
He said the timing of the bid was not driven by potential political implications for foreign investment after the October 12 general election.

Opposition party New Zealand First wants to limit foreign ownership of "strategic assets" to 25 percent. It would not force sales, but would require sellers of any holdings above that level to sell to New Zealand buyers.
New Zealand First is yet to release its full list of strategic assets, but in its indicative policy it did not include media ownership.
The Alliance's Corkery said in her statement: "New Zealand is being sold overseas piece by piece. We cannot get richer by selling everything."

Labour, the Alliance and New Zealand First can expect to win more than half the seats in parliament, according to opinion polls, but it remains unclear whether they could agree to form a government. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
